report.headline: Miami owns the trenches here
report.openingParagraph: Miami enters with the clearest edge on the field, and it starts at the line of scrimmage on both sides. The defining matchup is Miami offensive line versus the Clemson front, because it sets up everything else, the run game, the play-action shots, and the game script. Miami is No. 3 of 138 in line yards per carry at 3.89. Clemson is No. 135 at 3.46 allowed. That is the game’s loudest mismatch. The companion edge is just as important, Miami run defense against a Clemson run game that ranks No. 120 in rush success at 37%, facing a front that ranks No. 1 at 26% allowed.

sections.title: The matchup that matters most
paragraphs: This is not a lean. It is a mismatch, and a prominent one. Miami’s offense has a 57% success rate, No. 2 of 138, with 3.89 line yards and just 12% stuff rate. Clemson’s defense allows 49% rush success, No. 131 of 138, and 3.46 line yards, No. 135 of 138. Samson Okunlola fronts the unit edge, and Javian Mallory runs behind it. Watch yards before contact on Miami’s first ten carries. If Miami is clean early, Clemson’s linebackers, led by Sammy Brown and Jeremiah Alexander, are playing uphill all afternoon.

Darian Mensah is the accelerator once the run forces the issue. He has 1211 pass yds, 14 TD, 0 INT, and 11.4 Y/A. Miami also ranks No. 1 in pass success at 65%. Clemson is better on that side, No. 23 in pass success allowed at 34%, but this game still flows from Miami’s ability to stay ahead of schedule.

sections.title: Clemson faces a bad script
paragraphs: Clemson’s offense is balanced, struggling, and loses the line. The raw profile is poor across the board, 34% success, No. 133 of 138, 2.76 line yards, No. 113, and 23% passing-downs success, No. 124. Miami’s front answers with 26% rush success allowed, No. 1 of 138, 2.15 line yards allowed, No. 8, and 27% stuff rate, No. 9. Miami erases the run and pushes Clemson into passing downs, where the offense has been at its weakest.

That puts pressure on Gideon Davidson, T.J. Moore, and Clemson’s protection to create something against Marquise Lightfoot and a front that wins first contact. Watch tackles for loss early. If Miami is living in the backfield, Clemson’s 5.1 plays per drive profile is hard to escape.

sections.title: Projection and game shape
paragraphs: The model projects Miami by 10.9, with a projected score of Miami 29, Clemson 19, and confidence high. The shape is clear, Miami controls the line of scrimmage on both sides and shortens the game once ahead. The market moved from -12 to -15.5, while the total moved from 52.5 to 48. Rain sits at 54% from kickoff, with storm watch also in play. That points to more ball security emphasis, worse footing on cuts, and lower pass volume.

report.oneLineForCard: Miami has the trench edge on both sides, and that is the whole pregame picture.
